title: How to Start as a Primary ECT September 1, 2026
author: Mark Goodrich
summary: Mark Goodrich, writing for Primary Focus, offers a practical field guide for Early Career Teachers (ECTs) starting their first class in a UK primary school, covering the period from pre-term preparation through the end of the first week. He walks through concrete logistics—mining outgoing teachers and TAs for classroom intelligence, building a seating plan around SEND and behavioral considerations, and securing basic equipment like mini-whiteboards and a visualiser—before moving into first-day psychology: being firm on routines from the outset because it is far easier to relax later than to tighten up after starting too loose. Goodrich treats behavior as curriculum content that must be explicitly taught and co-created with students rather than assumed, and he pushes back against the instinct to skip academic content on day one. He flags the end of the first week as the moment boundary-testing begins in earnest and offers a specific classroom-management technique (front-loading the means of participation) borrowed from fellow educator Adam Boxer. The piece closes with an unusually candid argument against over-planning from scratch, framing reliance on shared schemes as a sustainable choice rather than a compromise, and insists new teachers protect their own time off.
points: Recommends mining the outgoing teacher and TA, not just school data, for the real intelligence needed to prepare a seating plan and classroom setup.
Argues for firmness on rules and routines from day one, since it's far easier to relax later than to retroactively tighten expectations once students have tested and found looseness.
Treats behavior as curriculum: good classroom behavior is a set of specific behaviors that must be explicitly taught and, where possible, co-created with students rather than simply imposed.
Flags the end of week one as the critical boundary-testing moment and recommends the 'front-loading the means of participation' technique for reducing calling-out and unclear instructions.
Pushes back against planning every lesson from scratch, calling it 'a recipe for burnout,' and advises new teachers to lean on shared schemes and protect their own time off.
quotes: Starting as an ECT in primary is a daunting feeling. Suddenly, you go from being a student teacher in someone else's class to having your own class.

As an ECT, you should not have been given a class with particular behavioural issues (and if you find out that you have been, this is a huge red flag about the school). However, any class in a mainstream primary school will have its issues.

It's best to be really firm on rules and routines at the outset when the children are sussing you out and considering whether to push the line. It's quite easy to relax a little later on if you have been too insistent on something.

I am a strong believer that behaviour should be regarded as part of the curriculum and needs to be taught just like everything else. In particular, good behaviour in school involves a whole set of individual behaviours which need to be taught.

By the end of the first week, some of your more enterprising students will be testing boundaries. It's important to reinforce them at this point because it will only get harder in weeks 2, 3 and thereafter.

This is a recipe for burnout and, in my opinion, a nonsensical way to run a school. Primary schools vary hugely in the amount of shared resources they have and their attitude to using them so you will need to scope this out quickly.
The basic idea is simple. You tell children how you want them to participate before telling them what you want them to do.
